argv:
Rewrite the text in dense corporate business jargon.

Replace concrete nouns with abstractions. Turn verbs into nominalisations:
prefer "the utilisation of" to "using". Use the passive voice so that no
sentence names who acts. Reach for "leverage", "synergy", "stakeholder",
"alignment", "operationalise", "value-add", and "at scale".

Hedge every claim. Add qualifying clauses that commit to nothing.

Keep the underlying facts of the original technically present, however deeply
buried. This column exists as a demonstration of what these habits cost.

request.user_prompt:
Rewrite the passage below according to your style instructions.

Output only the rewritten passage. Do not add a preamble, a title, an
explanation, or any commentary about the changes you made.

<passage>
The Millbrook Hollow City Council voted Tuesday night to approve an amended version of the parks and recreation line item, following a meeting that also touched on the long-delayed replacement of the Third Street bridge. According to a spokesperson for the mayor's office, the revised figure reflects "ongoing conversations" among council members, though the spokesperson declined to characterize those conversations further. A separate memo, attributed by two council staffers to the finance subcommittee, put the adjustment at approximately $340,000, a figure that a budget analyst who reviewed the memo said was "in the range we expected." Buried near the end of that same memo, and not raised by any council member during the meeting, was a line noting that the bridge's lead structural engineer had flagged a load-bearing crack serious enough to warrant closing the span to truck traffic within 90 days. The bridge project, which has appeared on the capital plan since at least 2019 and has already drawn 14 change orders, was not discussed in detail. Council member Dana Okafor, reached after the meeting, said only that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work, and I think residents should feel good about that."
</passage>

response.text:
In connection with Tuesday evening's proceedings, an amended version of the parks and recreation line item was, at a high level, approved by the Millbrook Hollow City Council, in a session that could also be characterized as having touched, to some extent, on the long-delayed replacement of the Third Street bridge, a capital-planning workstream whose status remains, in certain respects, subject to ongoing evaluation. It was indicated by a spokesperson for the mayor's office that the revised figure should be understood as reflective of "ongoing conversations" among stakeholders at the council level, although further characterization of those conversations was, for reasons not fully articulated, declined.

A separate memo — attribution of which has been variously assigned by two council staffers to the finance subcommittee, with the appropriate caveats around provenance — was said to place the adjustment in the neighborhood of $340,000, a quantum that, per a budget analyst engaged in a review capacity, could be considered broadly consistent with expectation-alignment, or "in the range we expected," without prejudice to further revision.

It should be noted, for completeness and in the interest of full stakeholder transparency, that a line item was situated toward the latter portion of said memo — and was not, for whatever reason, operationalized as a discussion point by any council member during the meeting proper — indicating that a load-bearing anomaly, characterized by the bridge's lead structural engineer as a crack of some structural significance, had been flagged as potentially warranting a truck-traffic closure of the span on a roughly 90-day horizon, pending further assessment.

The bridge initiative itself, a value-add capital undertaking that has appeared on the relevant planning documentation since at least 2019 and has, over that period, accumulated some 14 change orders, was not engaged with at a level of granular detail during this session. Council member Dana Okafor, when reached subsequent to the meeting's conclusion, offered a characterization to the effect that "the process worked the way it's supposed to work," adding, with what might be described as directional optimism, that residents should, on balance, feel good about that — a sentiment offered without further specificity as to actionable next steps or accountability mechanisms.
